prompt: Many developing countries have built their economies around large-scale international tourism. Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?
essay:
Whether tourism-led development pays depends almost entirely on a question the debate rarely asks: who owns the hotel? The same number of arrivals can leave a country with a middle class or with a coastline it no longer controls, and the difference is not in the tourists.

The case for the strategy is real, and it is not merely that tourism earns hard currency. It earns it in sectors where a poorer country genuinely competes. A nation cannot decide to have a semiconductor industry, but it can have a coastline, a climate and a ruin, and the capital needed to make those earn is modest by industrial standards. Tourism also employs across the whole skill range at once, which few other export sectors manage, and it builds infrastructure — airports, water treatment, roads — that residents use after the visitors have gone.

Where it goes wrong, it goes wrong through ownership. If the airline, the tour operator, the hotel and the excursion company are all foreign, a holiday can be sold, taken and paid for without much of the money touching the host economy at all; what remains is the wage bill for the lowest-paid roles and the environmental cost of the buildings. Add the exposure that comes from depending on a single sector, and a bad year abroad becomes a crisis at home.

So the advantages do outweigh the disadvantages, but only conditionally and unevenly. For a country that has legislated for local ownership, taxed the sector as an export rather than as a service, and kept some other industry alive alongside it, the arithmetic is comfortable. For one that has sold long leases on its best land and hoped, the visitors will still arrive — and most of what they spend will leave in the same week they do.
title: Mass tourism in developing economies
